newsitem.title: UK: "Queen of Hearts" to visit Angola mine victims.
newsitem.headline: "Queen of Hearts" to visit Angola mine victims.

text.p: Princess Diana will boost her "Queen of Hearts" image with a visit to Angola to see landmine victims while her divorced husband Charles battles to restore his popularity by turning himself into "the people's prince".
The glamorous princess, whose marriage to British royal heir Charles ended last August, will fly to Luanda at the weekend to back the Red Cross campaign against anti-personnel mines.
It will be gruelling. Angola has endured two decades of war and there are still an estimated nine million mines scattered around the country -- one for every man, woman and child.
Angola has the world's highest number of amputees and 24 people a day are being admitted to hospital with mine injuries.
A visit by the most photographed woman in the world was hailed by the British Red Cross as an unparalleled opportunity to raise awareness of anti-personnel mines.

"We are delighted that the Princess of Wales will be visiting the Red Cross operations in Angola, which has so many victims of these cruel weapons," said Mike Whitlam, director-general of the British Red Cross.
"Anti-personnel mines indiscriminately maim and kill 2,000 people a month around the world and so we are thrilled that the princess is joining us to highlight this humanitarian tragedy."
During her five-day trip, the princess will visit a Red Cross factory making artificial limbs, health centres and hospitals caring for the victims of Angola's war.

The Red Cross said Diana had decided to make the trip after attending the premiere of a new film version of Ernest Hemingway's novel "A Farewell to Arms". Half the performance's proceeds will go to the charity's anti-mine campaign.

In a landmark television interview at the end of 1995, Diana said she wanted to be the "queen of people's hearts". But after her divorce, she cut her links with more than 100 charities, the British Red Cross included.
A Red Cross spokeswoman dismissed suggestions of a new, permanent position for the princess with the charity, saying: "This is a one-off, there is no further commitment."
But the media said there has been a rethink of her role and that, if the Angola trip goes well, it could be followed by visits to trouble spots such as Bosnia and Afghanistan.
Prince Charles is fighting to regain the ground he has lost to Diana in the battle for public approval.

The BBC said on Friday that the prince had set up a strategy group to help improve his popularity and prepare him for the throne. The aim is to establish him as a "people's prince" committed to public service.

He is being groomed to take over some duties from his 70-year-old mother, Queen Elizabeth, including some of her state visits abroad. He will represent the queen at ceremonies in Hong Kong at the end of June marking the British colony's return to Chinese rule.
Buckingham Palace expects to mount a five-year campaign to persuade dubious Britons that Prince Charles is fit to be king, according to the Daily Mail.
It said the palace took the decision after a television poll showed Charles had slumped in popularity after his acrimonious divorce and affair with old flame Camilla Parker Bowles.
